name: Daily narration
blurb: Things you can say to yourself as you go through your day: hungry, thirsty, eating, wanting, going.

units.title: I am… I do…
units.blurb: Hunger, thirst, tiredness and everyday actions in the I-form
units.intro: A Latin verb ending tells you who is acting, so you rarely need a separate word for 'I'. The I-form ends in -ō (or -iō): _edō_ = I eat, _bibō_ = I drink, _dormiō_ = I sleep. Add _ego_ only for emphasis. The thing being eaten or drunk goes in the accusative: _cibum_ (food), _aquam_ (water). 'I am' is _sum_, and an adjective after it matches the speaker: _fessus sum_ (said by a man), _fessa sum_ (by a woman).

units.title: I want to…
units.blurb: volō / nōlō + infinitive, and post / ante + accusative
units.intro: To say 'I want to drink', Latin uses _volō_ with an infinitive: _bibere volō_ (or _volō bibere_). 'I don't want to' is _nōlō_ + infinitive. The infinitive ends in -re: _bibere, edere, dormīre, ambulāre_. For 'after' and 'before' use _post_ and _ante_ with the accusative: _post cibum_ = after the meal; _ante cibum_ = before the meal.

units.title: Narrating my day
units.blurb: Sequence words, times of day, and going home
units.intro: Link your actions with _prīmum_ (first), _deinde_ (then) and _postrēmō_ (finally). Times of day: _mane_ (in the morning), _nocte_ (at night), _hodiē_ (today). 'At home' is _domī_, and 'home' as a destination is _domum_ (no preposition): _domum eō_ = I go home.

units.title: What I did
units.blurb: The perfect tense: I ate, I drank, I slept, I went
units.intro: To say what you did, use the perfect tense. The I-form ends in -ī: _ēdī_ = I ate, _bibī_ = I drank, _dormīvī_ = I slept, _ambulāvī_ = I walked. The perfect stem has to be learned with each verb (_edō_ → _ēdī_, _surgō_ → _surrēxī_), so drill whole sentences rather than rules. Past-time words: _herī_ (yesterday), _hodiē_ (today). Don't confuse _edō_ (I eat) with _ēdī_ (I ate).

units.title: What I will do
units.blurb: The future tense: I will walk, I will eat, I will be
units.intro: To say what you will do, use the future tense. For -āre and -ēre verbs add -bō: _ambulābō_ = I will walk, _vidēbō_ = I will see. For -ere and -īre verbs the I-form ends in -am: _edam_ = I will eat, _bibam_ = I will drink, _dormiam_ = I will sleep. The future of _sum_ is _erō_. Time words: _crās_ (tomorrow), _mox_ (soon), _nunc_ (now).

units.title: Who does what to what
units.blurb: Subject, object and verb in whole sentences
units.intro: A Latin sentence tells you who does what with word endings, not word order. The subject is nominative (_puer_), the thing acted on is accusative (_pānem_), and the verb ending agrees with the subject: _puer pānem edit_ (the boy eats bread), _puerī pānem edunt_ (the boys eat bread). Because the endings carry the meaning, the same sentence can be written in any order. With _ego_, _tū_ and _nōs_ left out, the verb ending alone says who it is: _pānem edō_, _pānem edis_.

units.title: Asking questions
units.intro: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, add _-ne_ to the first word: _Edisne pānem?_ (Do you eat bread?). English needs 'do' or 'does'; Latin does not. To ask 'what?', use _quid_, and answer with the object: _Quid edis? Pānem edō._ Notice that the question uses the 'you' form (_edis_) and the answer the 'I' form (_edō_).

units.title: Yesterday I…
units.blurb: The past tense in every person
units.intro: The perfect tense tells what happened and is finished. Its endings are the same for every verb: -ī (I), -istī (you), -it (he/she), -imus (we), -istis (you all), -ērunt (they). The stem changes from verb to verb, so learn it with the verb: _edō → ēdī_, _videō → vīdī_, _veniō → vēnī_, _amō → amāvī_. Put a time word first and you have a story: _Herī pānem ēdī._

units.title: Tomorrow I will…
units.blurb: The future tense in every person
units.intro: The future tense says what will happen. For -āre and -ēre verbs it uses -bō, -bis, -bit, -bimus, -bitis, -bunt: _amābō_ (I will love), _habēbō_ (I will have). For -ere and -īre verbs the endings are -am, -ēs, -et, -ēmus, -ētis, -ent: _edam_ (I will eat), _audiam_ (I will hear). A time word like _crās_ (tomorrow) or _mox_ (soon) comes along to confirm it.

units.title: What used to happen
units.blurb: The imperfect: used to, was doing
units.intro: The imperfect tense describes what used to happen or was going on: -bam, -bās, -bat, -bāmus, -bātis, -bant (_amābam_, _habēbam_) or -ēbam, -ēbās… for -ere and -īre verbs (_edēbam_, _audiēbam_). Use it for habits (_cotīdiē_ = every day, _saepe_ = often) and for scenes you are describing: _puer pānem edēbat_ (the boy was eating bread). Use the perfect for a single finished event, the imperfect for a background or a habit.
